claims.text: Greg Short asserts that attributing others' success to luck is a form of victim mentality that prevents people from acknowledging the real causes of that success — disciplined preparation and hard work — and by doing so, insulates them from the changes in behavior that would actually close the gap.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
claims.mechanism: Framing success as luck relieves the observer of personal responsibility; no behavior change is required if the outcome is attributed to chance rather than effort.

claims.text: Greg Short argues that taking one step forward is categorically superior to standing still — not marginally better, but 100% better — because any forward movement is the direct opposite of inaction, regardless of how small the step is.
claims.speaker: Greg Short

claims.text: Greg Short claims that disciplined preparation — staying ready at all times — removes the need for reactive scramble when an opportunity or challenge appears; those who must 'get ready' have already fallen behind those who stayed ready.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
claims.speaker_term: stay ready so they didn't need to get ready
claims.mechanism: Sustained preparation eliminates the lag cost of reactive readiness; competitors who require a ramp-up period lose the window while the prepared person acts immediately.

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that people who use luck to explain others' success are jealous rather than analytical, and that proximity to people who invoke luck as an explanation is net-negative — removing them from one's environment is the correct response.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Person is actively pursuing a goal or mission

practices.text: Remove any person from your immediate environment who uses the word 'luck' to explain success; their framing is incompatible with forward progress.
Focus on taking one step forward rather than evaluating whether the step is large enough; forward movement in any increment is the correct baseline behavior.
